title: The Empire That Vanished
bullets: In 651 the last Sasanian king of kings, Yazdegerd III, was murdered in a miller's hut near Merv for his jewels, ending a thousand-year line of shahanshahs and the Persian Empire as a state.

The Arabs broke open Persia in a single decade: the field army shattered at al-Qadisiyyah in 636, Ctesiphon was plundered in 637, and the last great Sasanian army was destroyed at Nahavand in 642, the 'Victory of Victories.'
Yazdegerd's son Peroz III fled to the court of Tang China and spent his life lobbying a Chinese emperor for troops to retake his kingdom that never came.

The conquerors had a brilliant army but no state, so the Persian katibs kept their jobs and the new empire's tax registers were kept in Middle Persian because the winners could not read their own accounts.

Conversion was a slow drift, not a flood: most Persians stayed Zoroastrian for over a century, paying the jizya poll tax, while the priests wrote down their long-oral scriptures as their numbers slipped.
Non-Arab converts became mawali, second-class Muslims taxed and shut out despite Islam's promise of equality, and the resentment piled up fastest in the eastern province of Khurasan.
In 747 the Persian general Abu Muslim raised the black banners in Khurasan, and by 750 his army overthrew the Umayyads and put the Abbasids on the throne.

In 762 al-Mansur founded Baghdad as a perfect round city just up the Tigris from ruined Ctesiphon, quarrying the old capital and adopting Sasanian court ceremony to claim the inheritance of the kings of kings.
Al-Mansur had Abu Muslim murdered in 755, and a string of violent Persian revolts followed, including al-Muqanna the 'Veiled Prophet' who claimed to be divine before his fortress fell.

title: A Language Refuses to Die
bullets: Persia is essentially the only major land conquered by the early Arabs that kept its own language and made it a vehicle of high culture, while Egyptian, Syriac, and the rest faded into Arabic.

New Persian emerged around 800 from the spoken Persian of Khurasan, written in the easier Arabic alphabet and salted with Arabic loanwords but Persian to the bone, the way English stayed Germanic after borrowing French.

Around 750 the Persian convert Ibn al-Muqaffa translated Kalila wa-Dimna into elegant Arabic, smuggling Persian statecraft into the new culture as animal fables, and was later gruesomely executed by a governor he had offended.
The Abbasid-funded translation movement, centered on Baghdad's House of Wisdom, poured Greek, Indian, and Persian learning into Arabic just as that language reached the height of its prestige.
The Barmakids, a family of Persian converts from a Buddhist temple in Balkh, effectively ran the empire as viziers under Harun al-Rashid until he turned on them with terrifying suddenness around 803.
The Shu'ubiyya was a generations-long literary quarrel in which Persian writers, using Arabic, argued that the Persians were the cultural equals or betters of the Arabs who had conquered them.

In 821 the caliph rewarded the Persian general Tahir ibn Husayn with Khurasan, and his Tahirid descendants ran it as a near-independent dynasty, the first real crack in the caliphate's control of Persia.

Ya'qub ibn al-Layth, a coppersmith from Sistan, founded the Saffarid dynasty by 861 and nearly took Baghdad, and tradition makes him the first ruler to put New Persian poetry on the dais beside the throne.

title: The Samanid Renaissance
bullets: The Samanids, a Persian dynasty claiming descent from the Sasanian kings, ruled from Bukhara in Transoxiana and made reviving Persian high culture a deliberate, money-backed policy.
Their capital Bukhara was called 'the dome of Islam in the East,' a city of mosques, bazaars, and a library so famous the young Avicenna described it as a wonder.

The renaissance ran on silver: Samanid dirhams from Central Asian mines have been dug up by the hundreds of thousands in Viking hoards in Scandinavia and Russia, so the same coins that paid Rudaki ended up under Swedish farms.
Rudaki, the blind court poet called the 'father of Persian poetry,' proved the new written language could carry poetry as sophisticated as anything in Arabic.

Ferdowsi spent roughly thirty years finishing the Shahnameh around 1010, an epic of about 50,000 couplets telling Persia's entire mythical and royal past, written in deliberately pure Persian to prove the language could carry the nation's memory alone.
The Shahnameh's heroes became permanent cultural touchstones, above all the champion Rustam, who unknowingly kills his own son Sohrab in single combat in the epic's most heartbreaking tale.

The Samanid world produced Avicenna, whose Canon of Medicine was a European textbook for six hundred years, plus al-Biruni, al-Razi who distinguished smallpox from measles, and al-Khwarizmi, whose name and book-title became the words algorithm and algebra.

The Ghaznavids, Turkish slave-soldiers turned kings, snuffed out the Samanids but ran a thoroughly Persian court, and Mahmud of Ghazni carried the Persianate model east into India even as he raided its temples seventeen times.

title: The Persian Intermezzo
bullets: The Buyids came from Daylam, the rugged Caspian highlands that were among the last parts of Persia to be conquered, and rose from a family of mountain mercenaries into kings.

In 945 the Buyid Ahmad marched into Baghdad and took it, and the dynasty kept the Sunni caliph as a powerless figurehead, his name on the coins and in the prayers while they held the army and the treasury as amir al-umara.

The arrangement carried a delicious irony: the Buyids were Shia keeping a Sunni caliph as a pet, propping him up rather than replacing him because they needed his Sunni legitimacy more than a co-religionist on the throne.

The Sunni-Shia split went back to the question of who should lead after Muhammad died in 632, the Sunnis favoring chosen elders and the Shia holding that leadership belonged by right to Ali and his descendants.

Adud al-Dawla, the greatest Buyid, ruled in the 970s and revived the ancient title shahanshah, 'king of kings,' announcing that the old Persian imperial idea had come back to the very capital built on Ctesiphon's bones.

Under tolerant Buyid patronage the intellectual life of Twelver Shiism came of age, with Shaykh al-Mufid systematizing its theology and the canonical hadith collections compiled, planting the seed of Shia Iran half a millennium before it flowered.
Historians call the episode the Iranian or Buyid Intermezzo, a label applied in hindsight to a real resurgence of Persian language, titles, and political power across the tenth century.
The Buyids were undone by their military weakness: their Daylamite infantry was being eclipsed by Turkish cavalry, and in 1055 a migrating nation of free Turkish nomads would brush them aside.

title: Turks Who Ruled in Persian
bullets: The Seljuks were Oghuz Turks, nomadic horse-archers off the Central Asian steppe whose Turkic language was no relation at all to Indo-European Persian, who conquered Persia and then governed it more Persian than the Persians.

After smashing the Ghaznavids from 1037, the Seljuk leader Tughril Beg marched into Baghdad in 1055, drove out the Shia Buyids, and had himself proclaimed sultan, inventing the template of a Turkish warrior-king ruling in the caliph's name.

Having no government of their own, the Seljuks hired the Persian katibs, so the Turks supplied the cavalry and the Persians supplied the chancery, building a Persian empire with a Turkish army on top.

Nizam al-Mulk served as vizier for about thirty years under two sultans and effectively ran the empire, and his Siyasatnama, the 'Book of Government,' fused the Sasanian ideal of the just king with Islamic duty and hard practical advice.

He founded the state-funded Nizamiyya madrasas, the grandest established in Baghdad in 1067, making the religious college a deliberate instrument of the state and shaping Sunni higher learning for the rest of the period.
At Manzikert in 1071 Sultan Alp Arslan crushed the Byzantine army and captured the emperor, opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement and beginning the long process that made it modern Turkey.

Omar Khayyam, famous in his own time as a mathematician and astronomer, led the team that produced the Jalali calendar around 1079, more accurate than the Gregorian calendar Europe would adopt five centuries later.
Seljuk builders perfected the four-iwan mosque plan, its supreme example the Friday Mosque of Isfahan, the model for Persian mosques for the next eight hundred years.

In 1092 Nizam al-Mulk was assassinated and Sultan Malik-Shah died within weeks, fracturing the empire, but the Seljuks had made Persian the prestige language of the whole Persianate world, spread overwhelmingly by Turks who were not ethnically Persian at all.

title: The Castles in the Mountains
bullets: The Nizari Ismailis were a Shia splinter of a Shia splinter, an Ismaili branch with an esoteric inner doctrine, who broke from Fatimid Egypt in 1094 over the disputed succession of Nizar.

Hasan-i Sabbah, a brilliant Persian missionary born in Qom, seized the mountain fortress of Alamut in 1090 and built a network of impregnable eagle's-nest strongholds embedded inside the hostile Seljuk empire.

Unable to field an army, the Nizaris turned targeted political murder into a disciplined instrument of state, killing the one general or vizier holding a campaign together, usually with a dagger and often at the cost of the killer's own life.
By tradition their first famous victim was Nizam al-Mulk, the Seljuk vizier who had built the madrasa system in part to fight Ismaili propaganda, struck down in 1092 by a killer disguised as a Sufi.

The English word assassin derives from Hashishin, 'hashish-users,' almost certainly a slur thrown at the sect rather than a description of their habits, with no good evidence the Nizaris drugged their agents.

The lurid 'Old Man of the Mountain' legend of a secret drugged garden, told most influentially by Marco Polo decades after Alamut fell, is judged by modern scholarship to be Orientalist romance, not history.
Far from a drug cult, Alamut housed a famous library and sheltered Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, one of the greatest scientists of the medieval world, who spent decades doing his work there.

In 1256 the strategy finally met its match: Hulagu Khan's Mongols, with the patience and siege engines the Seljuks never had, took Alamut and methodically destroyed the fortresses, though the Nizari faith survives today as a worldwide community led by the Aga Khan.

title: The Inner Path
bullets: Sufism is the mystical, inward dimension of Islam, concerned with the inner experience of and ecstatic nearness to God, a current within both Sunni and Shia rather than a separate sect.
Al-Ghazali, the most celebrated scholar in Islam and holder of the Nizamiyya chair in Baghdad, suffered a breakdown around 1095, walked away from everything, and wandered a decade as a Sufi seeker.

His masterwork, the Ihya ulum al-din, reconciled the outer law with the inner path and, coming from the establishment's own greatest authority, made Sufism respectable at the center of mainstream Sunni piety.

In The Incoherence of the Philosophers, al-Ghazali attacked the rationalist tradition built on Avicenna and Aristotle, a critique often credited with checking the prestige of pure philosophy in the eastern Islamic world.

Attar of Nishapur, a druggist by trade, wrote the Conference of the Birds around 1177, in which thirty birds seeking their king the Simurgh discover that si murgh, 'thirty birds,' is themselves all along.
Nizami Ganjavi composed the Khamsa, five long poems that defined the Persian romance, including Layla and Majnun, sometimes called the Romeo and Juliet of the East.

Rumi, the supreme voice of Persian mysticism, was born near Balkh around 1207, fled the Mongol advance as a boy, and wrote his Persian masterpieces in Konya in Anatolia, proving the culture had become portable enough to flower in exile.
After his electrifying friendship with Shams of Tabriz around 1244, Rumi poured out the Masnavi, a six-volume poem of some 25,000 couplets so revered it is called 'the Quran in the Persian tongue.'

Sufi brotherhoods called tariqas, including Rumi's whirling-dervish Mevlevi order, spread across Persia and became the lived religion of ordinary people, decentralizing faith into thousands of lodges that no army could destroy.

title: The Brittle Colossus
bullets: Khwarazm was a rich, irrigated land on the delta of the Amu Darya near the Aral Sea, and its rulers, the Khwarazm-Shahs, began as Turkic provincial governors serving the Seljuks before making themselves independent.
In a few decades the Khwarazm-Shahs swallowed most of Persia and Central Asia, assembling by around 1210 the largest empire in the Muslim world, colossal on a map but a hollow shell underneath.
Unlike the Seljuk synthesis cured over generations, the Khwarazmian army was a distrusted mass of recently recruited tribal Turks and its conquered cities were too freshly swallowed to be loyal.
Its ruler, Ala al-Din Muhammad II, distrusted his own generals, quarreled with the Abbasid caliph he tried to depose, and had no real strategy for defending a wide and shallow realm.

Far to the east, Genghis Khan had welded the steppe tribes into a disciplined war machine, conquered northern China, and, wanting trade rather than war, sent a large commercial caravan and envoys to Khwarazm.

In 1218 the governor of the frontier city of Otrar seized the entire Mongol caravan, called the merchants spies, and had them killed, then Muhammad refused to hand him over and abused the embassy Genghis sent.

That single act of arrogance at a frontier town almost no one remembers turned the deadliest army in the world from facing east toward China to facing west toward Persia, in 1219 and in a mood to annihilate.

title: The End of the World
bullets: The Mongol army was the most disciplined and mobile force in the world, mounted archers who could cover a hundred miles a day, used feigned retreats, learned siege warfare fast, and made deliberate terror a strategy.
Muhammad II garrisoned his cities separately rather than massing his forces, handing Genghis a sequence of isolated sieges, then fled and died sick and abandoned on a Caspian island in 1220.
Bukhara, the old Samanid capital, fell in early 1220, and tradition has Genghis riding into the great mosque and ordering the Qur'ans trampled under his cavalry's hooves.

In 1221 the Mongols destroyed the great Khurasan cities of Merv, Nishapur, and Herat so thoroughly it changed the region's demography for centuries, the chroniclers describing pyramids of stacked heads.

The two Persian chroniclers of the conquest, Juvayni and Rashid al-Din, both served the Mongols, and their body counts in the hundreds of thousands are the inflated language of trauma rather than a census.

The quietest damage may have done the most lasting harm: the wrecking of the qanats, the underground irrigation channels whose maintainers were dead or gone, turned whole districts to desert that never recovered.
Jalal al-Din Mangburni, the shah's brave son, waged a decade-long fugitive war before being killed in 1231 by a Kurdish bandit who had no idea who he was.

In 1256 Genghis's grandson Hulagu took Alamut and destroyed the Assassins, then in 1258 sacked Baghdad and had the caliph al-Musta'sim rolled in a carpet and trampled, ending a 500-year institution in an afternoon.

In 1260 the Egyptian Mamluks defeated a reduced Mongol force at Ayn Jalut in Palestine, the first major check in the west, fixing the boundary of a Persia now conquered twice and seemingly extinguished.

title: The Conquerors Convert
bullets: Hulagu's realm became the Ilkhanate, a Mongol military aristocracy ruling Persia from Tabriz as a far-western province of a world-empire, its early khans non-Muslim and strikingly indifferent to Islam.

Hopeless at running states, the Mongols reached for the same Persian secretaries the Arabs had, and that single fiscal fact got Persian civilization back inside the empire that had wrecked it, faster than before.

Nasir al-Din al-Tusi transferred from the Assassins to Hulagu and persuaded the man who had just burned Baghdad's libraries to fund the Maragha observatory from 1259, whose Tusi couple turns up later in the work of Copernicus.
In 1295 the seventh Ilkhan, Ghazan, a great-great-grandson of Genghis raised a Buddhist, converted to Islam, declared it the state religion, and brought much of the Mongol aristocracy with him.

Ghazan's vizier Rashid al-Din, a Persian physician born Jewish, rebuilt the Mongol state on Persian lines, reforming the coinage and tax system and resettling the very land his patrons' grandfathers had ruined.
Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tawarikh has a fair claim to be the first true world history, using the Mongol empire's reach to write the history of everyone, the Chinese, Jews, Franks, and Indians alike.

The Mongol-opened roads to Yuan China brought Chinese motifs west, and out of that fusion the Persian miniature crystallized in the Ilkhanid workshops, one of the supreme achievements of Islamic visual art.
The court commissioned the monumental Great Mongol Shahnameh, the Persian national epic lavishly illustrated for the converted descendants of the men who had tried to erase that very identity.
When the last effective Ilkhan, Abu Said, died heirless in 1335, the state came apart into squabbling successor dynasties, leaving Persia battered but unmistakably itself.

title: Skulls and Tilework
bullets: Hafez of Shiraz, writing ghazals under the Muzaffarid splinter-state, brought the lyric to a pitch of compression where a couplet is at once a drinking song, a love poem, mystical theology, and satire, and Iranians still consult his Divan as an oracle.
Timur, the Turco-Mongol called Tamerlane, took Samarkand around 1370 and, unable to claim the title of khan, ruled as an amir behind a Genghisid puppet while launching thirty-five years of conquest.
Timur devastated Persia a second time in the 1380s and 1390s, sacking Baghdad twice and Isfahan, and building towers of skulls outside the walls as a deliberate instrument of policy.

At Ankara in 1402 Timur shattered the Ottoman army and captured Sultan Bayezid I 'the Thunderbolt,' who died in captivity, setting back the rise of the Ottoman Empire by a generation; Timur died on the road to invade China in 1405.

Timur poured the deported craftsmen of half of Asia into rebuilding Samarkand, raising the over-ambitious Bibi-Khanym Mosque and his own turquoise-domed tomb, the Gur-e-Amir, ancestor of the Taj Mahal.
Timur's son Shah Rukh ruled forty years from Herat over the Timurid renaissance, a Turkic dynasty patronizing Persian culture with total devotion.

Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg built a great observatory at Samarkand around 1424 whose star catalogue was the most accurate between Ptolemy and the sixteenth century, while al-Kashi computed pi to sixteen decimal places.
The Persian miniature reached its summit in the Herat workshops under the painter Bihzad, whose lifelike figures made him so famous that later forgers signed his name to lesser works.

Jami, the last of the great classical Persian poets, closed the canon at Herat, while the minister Ali-Shir Nava'i proved Chagatai Turkish a worthy literary language, signaling Persian's absolute dominance had a horizon.

title: The Red-Heads and the Boy King
bullets: By 1500 Persia was a patchwork of rivals: the lingering successor dynasties, including the militant Shia Sarbadars, and two great Turkmen confederations.

The Aq Qoyunlu or 'White Sheep' Turkmen beat the Black Sheep and under Uzun Hasan dominated western Persia, even negotiating an alliance with Venice against the Ottomans, before fracturing into succession wars.
Around 1300 the holy man Shaykh Safi al-Din founded the Safaviyya Sufi order at Ardabil, a quietist brotherhood that stayed out of politics for generations.

Over the fifteenth century the Safaviyya radicalized into a militant Shiism and attracted the rootless Turkmen tribes, who came to regard the hereditary sheikh as a near-divine figure worth dying for.

These followers were the Qizilbash, 'red-heads,' named for a tall red cap traditionally said to have twelve folds for the twelve Imams of Twelver Shiism, one of the most dangerous fighting forces in the region.

Ismail's grandfather and father were both killed fighting these enemies, so the last viable heir of the Safavid line spent his childhood in hiding, smuggled from place to place by Qizilbash who believed he was a messiah.
In 1499 the twelve-year-old Ismail came out of hiding, gathered the Qizilbash, and at the Battle of Sharur in 1501 defeated the fractured White Sheep army and cleared the road to Tabriz.

At fourteen Ismail had himself proclaimed Shah, reaching past the Mongols and Arabs to the pre-Islamic title of king of kings, and decreed Twelver Shiism the official religion of an overwhelmingly Sunni land.

The forced conversion to Shiism, enforced over a century with bloodshed, is the origin of Iran today as the great Shia power of the Muslim world, a distinction decreed by a teenage warlord-mystic in Tabriz in 1501.
